cards.lead: Tailored skin clothing of the North American Arctic
cards.note: The earliest source-backed evidence here is Saqqaq sewing in Greenland, c. 2400-900 BC, not c. 2500 BCE, and the sources opened do not show that the technique came from Siberia or was developed locally. The Thule-period garments and the Bering Strait claims were not sourced.
cards.name: Stitched skin clothing of the Saqqaq culture, Greenland
cards.summary: Saqqaq hunters of Disko Bay, Greenland, sewed fitted skin garments with advanced stitching, preserved in frozen sites from about 2400 BC.
cards.description: Frozen Saqqaq sites at Qeqertasussuk and Qajaa in Disko Bay preserve skin fragments, including a stocking with its fur on the inside and a repaired hole at the big toe. The stitching shows advanced sewing technique, and the two sites together cover the whole Saqqaq era in Greenland, about 2400 to 900 BC.
cards.origin_note: The sources show Saqqaq sewing skill in Greenland but do not say whether it was brought from earlier Arctic peoples or developed locally, so independence is not settled.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the spread of this clothing to later Arctic peoples is not yet sourced.

events.label: c. 2400-900 BC
events.statement: Skin fragments from the frozen Saqqaq sites of Qeqertasussuk and Qajaa in Disko Bay show advanced sewing, and the Saqqaq era there is dated c. 2400-900 BC.
events.quote: Skin fragments, including the foot of a stocking, show the advanced sewing techniques of the Saqqaq

sources.title: The Frozen Saqqaq Sites of Disko Bay, West Greenland: Qeqertasussuk and Qajaa (2400-900 BC)
One of Greenland's first inhabitants had a hole in their sock

open_questions: Whether the Early Arctic Small Tool sewing came from Siberia or was developed in place, and what the Bering Strait sites show, is not yet sourced.
The Thule-period garments (double-layer caribou parkas and sealed gut coats) need their own sources.
The Disko Bay coordinates are approximate and were not taken from a fetched source.

cards.lead: Fat-burning stone lamps in Ice Age Europe
cards.note: The lamp date is c. 40,000 to 11,000 years ago across the Upper Palaeolithic, per the de Beaune and White caption, not c. 40,000 to 15,000. The sources put the earliest uncontested lamp in the Gravettian at Laugerie-Haute, so origin is unknown here rather than first known: no source compares other regions.
cards.name: Fat-burning stone lamps of the Upper Palaeolithic
cards.summary: Hollowed stone lamps burning animal fat gave steady light in Upper Palaeolithic Europe, found mainly in south-west France, from about 40,000 years ago.
cards.description: Stone lamps burning animal fat on a wick were used through the Upper Palaeolithic, from about 40,000 to 11,000 years ago, and are found mainly in south-west France. A sandstone object found at Lascaux in 1895 was the first recognised as a lamp, after analysis of its sooty cup revealed animal fat-based combustibles. The earliest uncontested lamp is Gravettian at Laugerie-Haute, a date the sources opened do not give.
cards.origin_note: The sources date the lamps but do not compare them with lamps elsewhere, such as the Arctic or the Near East, so independence is not settled.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the later spread of the lamp is not yet sourced.

events.label: c. 38,000 to 9,000 BCE (40,000 to 11,000 years ago)
events.statement: Lamps appear in all eras of the Upper Palaeolithic, 40,000 to 11,000 years ago; converted from BP by subtracting from 1950.
events.quote: Lamps appear in all eras of the Upper Paleolithic (40 000 to 11 000 years ago)
events.locator: Caption, Ice Age lamps (quoting de Beaune and White)

sources.title: Stone Lamps of the Palaeolithic (reproducing de Beaune and White, Scientific American)

open_questions: The Gravettian lamp at Laugerie-Haute and the Aurignacian candidates (de Beaune 1993) need their primary publications for dates.
The 1987 Current Anthropology paper by de Beaune was not readable from the fetcher or the web fetch tool, so its claims rest on secondary pages.
Lamps elsewhere (Saqqaq blubber lamps in Greenland, the Near East) are separate origins to check.
The Southwest France coordinates are approximate and were not taken from a fetched source.

cards.note: The earliest dated ondols in the source opened are 3rd century BC in Primorye and northeast Korea and 2nd century BC in southern Korea, not an origin in the northern peninsula at c. 300 BCE. The Unggi c. 1000 BCE and Sonbong c. 5000 BC claims found online were not confirmed by any fetchable scholarly source.
cards.name: Ondol heated floors in Primorye and Korea
cards.summary: Stone floors heated by flues from the kitchen fire appeared in Primorye and northeast Korea by the 3rd century BC, and in southern Korea in the 2nd.
cards.description: Krounovka culture dwellings in Primorye, northeast Korea and Manchuria had ondol flue-heated floors of similar construction by the 3rd century BC. Kim's analysis of 49 dwellings at Bangiri and Neukdo Island in southeastern Korea argues that ondols reached the southern peninsula in the 2nd century BC under Krounovka influence.
cards.origin_note: Kim's paper argues that the southern Korean ondols followed Krounovka building traditions, a transmission the author ties to migration, though it rests on dated sites rather than a direct record of transfer.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the later spread of the ondol across Korea is not yet sourced.

events.label: 3rd century BC
events.statement: Ondols of similar construction are known from the Krounovka culture in Primorye, northeast Korea and Manchuria as early as the 3rd century BC.
events.quote: In the areas of the Krounovka (Tuanjie) culture in Primorye, Northeastern Korea and Manchuria, ondols of similar construction have been known as early as the 3rd century BC.

events.label: 2nd century BC
events.statement: Early ondol dwellings appear in the southernmost part of Korea, at Neukdo Island, in the 2nd century BC, which Kim's comparison of dated sites supports.
events.quote: confirm the hypothesis of the appearance in the 2nd century BC of dwellings with early ondols in the southernmost part of Korea

sources.title: The Ondol Heating Systems in Dwellings on Neukdo Island, Korea, and at the Krounovka Sites in Primorye, Russia (300-100 BC)

open_questions: The Unggi (North Korea) ondol of about 1000 BC and the Sonbong site of about 5000 BC come only from encyclopaedic pages and need excavation reports.
The Greek and Roman hypocaust, which the lead names as a separate and possibly earlier origin, needs a scholarly source before comparison.
The Neukdo Island and Primorye coordinates are approximate and were not taken from a fetched source.

cards.note: The earliest source-backed date is 3 November 1492, in Columbus's journal, not the placeholder year 1000. No archaeological or linguistic evidence for an earlier hammock was found in the sources opened, and the Royal Navy 1597 date was not found.
cards.name: Hammock of the Caribbean and tropical America
cards.summary: A woven hanging bed used across the Caribbean; Columbus recorded it in 1492, and the word is probably of Taino origin.
cards.description: Columbus's journal for 3 November 1492 is the first direct European reference to hammocks, which he saw in use on the Caribbean islands. Later explorers and sailors described hammocks across the Americas through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. No earlier archaeological find was located in the sources opened.
cards.origin_note: The thesis gives the word as probably of Taino origin but says little is known of hammock origins; no source opened settles whether the form was independent or spread.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; its adoption at sea is only partly sourced.

events.label: 3 November 1492
events.statement: Columbus makes the first direct European reference to hammocks in his journal entry for 3 November 1492.
events.quote: On November 3, 1492, he made his first direct reference to hammocks,
events.locator: Chapter on hammock history, citing Columbus's journal

open_questions: Any pre-1492 age for the hammock needs archaeological or linguistic evidence; none was found.
The Royal Navy adoption date of 1597 was not found. The thesis gives a fleet of 3000 men receiving 300 hammocks in 1624 and says the English navy supplied most over-sea vessels by 1629.
Columbus's journal and Oviedo's 1535 description were not opened directly; the Caribbean coordinates are approximate.

cards.note: The Thor is dated circa 1907 and made by the Hurley Machine Company in Chicago. Priority as the first electric washer is disputed, so the lead's 1908 date and its claim of first known status are not settled by the sources opened.
cards.name: Thor electric washing machine, Chicago
cards.summary: The Thor electric washer, made by the Hurley Machine Company in Chicago around 1907, survives in a museum collection as an early electric washing machine.
cards.description: The Hurley Machine Company of Chicago manufactured the Thor electric washing machine, patented by Alva J. Fisher, and The Henry Ford holds an example dated circa 1907. The sources opened do not settle whether it was the first electric washer, and the household spread of powered washing is not yet sourced.
cards.origin_note: The museum record gives manufacture and patent only; the priority claims for the first electric washer are disputed and no opened source settles them.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the labour and household effects are not yet sourced.

events.label: c. 1907
events.statement: The Thor electric washing machine, patented by Alva J. Fisher, was manufactured by the Hurley Machine Co. in Chicago, circa 1907.
events.quote: Patented by Alva J. Fisher. Manufactured by Hurley Machine Co. of Chicago, Illinois

sources.title: Thor Electric Washing Machine, circa 1907 (object THF109595)

open_questions: Priority: the earliest electric washers and the Fisher patent date of 1910 need fetched sources before any first claim is made.
Competing makers, the hand-cranked drum machines before them, and rates of household adoption through the century are not yet sourced.

cards.note: The Cuello sweat bath is dated to 900 BC through a secondary citation, but no source opened shows that the Maya sweat bath was independent of other traditions, so origin is changed to unknown. The Hammond and Bauer 2001 note, which is the primary source, was not readable.
cards.name: Sweat bath in the Maya lowlands
cards.summary: Maya builders at Cuello, Belize, made small ritual sweat baths by about 900 BC, used for childbirth, fertility, purification and healing.
cards.description: Sweat baths, or pib na, were small ritual spaces in the Maya lowlands associated with childbirth, fertility, purification, healing and the Underworld. Pugh dates a sweat bath at Cuello, Belize, to 900 BC, citing Hammond and Bauer's 2001 report, which stood on the eastern side of a plaza.
cards.origin_note: The sources describe Mesoamerican sweat baths but do not compare them with Old World baths or North American sweat lodges, so independence is not shown.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead; the three-thousand-year continuity and modern use are not yet sourced.

events.label: 900 BC
events.statement: A sweat bath at Cuello, Belize, stood on the eastern side of a plaza and is dated to 900 BC, as cited by Pugh.
events.quote: An earlier sweat bath datinged to 900 BC at Cuello stood on the eastern side of a plaza
events.locator: Section on round buildings and sweat baths

sources.title: Social Complexity and the Middle Preclassic Lowland Maya

open_questions: Read Hammond and Bauer (2001), Antiquity 75: 683-684, to check the 900 BC date; its text was behind a paywall.
The 16th-century accounts of sweat bath use among the Aztecs and Maya, and later Maya examples, need their own fetched sources.
The Cuello coordinates are approximate and were not taken from a fetched source.
